title: A Single Signal May Be Our Best Hint of Dark Matter Yet
mediaSource: LUX-ZEPLIN detector underground laboratory South Dakota dark matter galaxy liquid xenon science experiment

scenes.title: We may have caught dark matter
scenes.narration: Dark matter appears to make up most of the matter in the universe, yet we have never detected it directly. Now one mysterious particle event has appeared in a detector deep underground.

scenes.title: One strange collision
scenes.narration: Inside the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment, scientists recorded a faint flash of light together with a nuclear recoil in liquid xenon. Known background signals have not yet explained the event.

scenes.title: Could it have been a WIMP?
scenes.narration: The signal looks similar to what physicists expect if a WIMP, one of the leading dark matter candidates, collided with an atomic nucleus. If confirmed, it could be historic.

scenes.title: But this is not a discovery yet
scenes.narration: There is one major problem: only a single event has been seen. Physics requires extremely strong statistical evidence before scientists can call something a discovery.

scenes.title: Why is dark matter so hard to find?
scenes.narration: Dark matter does not emit or reflect light. We infer that it exists from gravity, galaxy rotation and other effects, but we still do not know what it is actually made of.

scenes.title: Could one signal change physics?
scenes.narration: Dark matter is thought to make up about 85 percent of all matter in the universe. If this event turns out to be real, one of modern physics' biggest mysteries could finally begin to unravel.
